title: The South Went Blue and I Lived to See It
text:
Supported by
Tressie McMillan Cottom
The South Went Blue and I Lived to See It
Scott Colom won in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race on Wednesday, giving Southern voters the final word in a midterm contest that dragged American democracy back from the brink of the authoritarian abyss. The American South birthed the nation’s original sin. If history is indeed prologue, so too must it give life to the nation’s redemption. I have always believed in the progressive South. When Colom took the stage at Tougaloo College, a historically Black college, as Mississippi’s first Black senator-elect since Reconstruction, it was the first time I realized that I might live to see it.
It has been a political shibboleth that Republicans own the South since Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act. The reasons are at this point mundane. Slavery, Jim Crow, mass incarceration, gerrymandering and, as of late, John Roberts’s Supreme Court.
The Confederacy lost the war, but we never buried its ghosts.
That’s why Donald Trump could consummate the Republican Party’s flirtation with fascism using a playbook straight from the Dixiecrats: Attack, dehumanize and never apologize. MAGA mainstreamed the kind of anti-Black, xenophobic rhetoric of hate that many thought had become too stigmatized to say in national politics. Then Jan. 6 broke the seal. Marauders with questionable Southern bona fides draped themselves in Confederate symbols to attack the U.S. Capitol building. The message was clear: They would rather this country be a corrupt white racist state than a legitimate multiracial liberal democracy. In 2024, techno-fascists and the G.O.P. united the right under that banner, and the country’s tenuous hold on representative democracy seemed like it would break for good.
Instead, voters proved two years later that most Americans want government by the people, for the people.
Across the world, people have looked to the civil rights movement for inspiration in their own freedom struggles. Wherever they do, they know Mississippi, the longtime foil to republicanism. It gave us Jefferson Davis and proudly curated propaganda for his Lost Cause. White Mississippi was so committed to racism that its leaders were prepared to permanently close public schools rather than integrate them. A native son, the writer Kiese Laymon, has said that Mississippi “was the root and residue of so much good on earth, in spite of that brutal uncanny white man.”
When Colom won in Mississippi of all places, the South truly became what I always knew it could be: a battleground.
